To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a new approach that allows for the localization of gap junctions in whole cells at both the light and electron microscopic levels.

tyramide signal amplified immunofluorescence and fluorescence photooxidized immunolabeling can be used for correlative light microscopy and high‐voltage transmission electron microscopy of gap junctions.
we have developed a method for specific labeling of connexions in cells that can be correlated with light microscopic images.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of gap junctions and the gap junction proteins (connexins).
the development of new methods to study the structure and function of gap junction proteins at the light and electron microscopic levels.
the use of correlative microscopy to study gap junction proteins in cultured cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the connexin43 gap junctional protein in NRK cells is localized to the lateral plasma membrane and that the connexins are not present on intracellular vesicles.

the use of the tyramide signal‐amplification technique in combination with fluorescence photooxidation provides a powerful tool for high‐resolution immunolabeling of proteins in whole cells for correlative light‐ and electron microscopic imaging.
the use of a combination of the tyramide signal enhancement and the photooxidation techniques allows for the specific labeling of connexon 43 at a high‐resolution level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the combination of these two techniques, tyramide signal and fluorescence photooxidization, is the most effective method to date for the specific localization and identification of gap junction proteins at the electron microscopic resolution level.
the use of tyramides and photooxidation allows us to localize gap junctions in whole cells at both light and electron microscopic levels.
fluorescence photooxidation can be used for high‐resolution immunocytochemical labeling of proteins in whole cells and tissues for correlative light‐ and electron microscopic imaging.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the combination of tyrosinase‐mediated fluorescence photooxidation and high‐voltage transmission electron microscopy (HVEM) provides a method to label and localize proteins in cells at high resolution.
we can now perform high‐resolution localization studies for proteins that are not easily labeled with colloidal gold.
it is possible to use immunocytochemical techniques to localize gap junction proteins in fixed, ultrathin‐sectioned tissue culture cells.
